questions.q: What does CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Name ON TableName (Column) do?
options: Physically sorts the table's rows by that column
Creates a separate lookup structure without changing row order
Deletes the existing clustered index and leaves the table unindexed
Only works on temp tables
questions.explain: A clustered index determines the actual physical storage order of the table's rows.

questions.q: How many clustered indexes can a single table have?
options: Only one
Up to five
Unlimited, same as nonclustered
Zero — clustered indexes are built automatically and can't be created manually
questions.explain: Since a clustered index defines physical row order, a table can only be sorted one way at a time.

questions.q: What does INCLUDE do in CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ... (Column) INCLUDE (OtherColumn)?
options: Adds OtherColumn to the index's leaf pages without making it part of the sort key
Makes OtherColumn part of the sort key, just like Column
Includes every column in the table automatically
Converts the nonclustered index into a clustered one
questions.explain: INCLUDE stores extra columns alongside the index entries so queries can read them without a lookup, while only Column defines the sort order.

options: A nonclustered index (often with INCLUDE) that satisfies a query entirely without touching the underlying table
A clustered index that covers every column in the table
An index that automatically rebuilds itself nightly
A backup copy of an existing index
questions.explain: When an index's key plus INCLUDE columns contain everything a query needs, SQL Server never has to follow the pointer back to the full row.

questions.q: How many nonclustered indexes can a table have, compared to clustered?
options: Many nonclustered indexes are allowed, versus only one clustered index
Exactly the same limit applies to both
Only one nonclustered index is allowed per table
Nonclustered indexes are unlimited only if there is no clustered index
questions.explain: Each nonclustered index is a separate structure, so a table can have many of them tuned for different lookup patterns.
